ARLINA
A Salute to Transportation
•.DOING A JOB FOR THE NATION!
This is a war of transportation. The materials of war are now being produced in great
quantities. Men are being trained for the Army and Navy in every corner of the land.
Knitting this vast continent together... moving men and materials of war from one
part of the United States to another with utmost speed... and then to the battle grounds
overseas... that is the job of transportation.... And it is a job that is being well done!
We of United Air Lines are as proud of the job
others are doing as we are of our own. And that
goes for the other airlines, the railroads, the mer-
chant marine, the bus and truck lines.
Naturally, we know more about our own indus-
try than we do about the others in the transporta-
tion field. With fewer planes, we, the airlines of
the country, are maintaining schedules that com
pare favorably with peacetime ones...and our
operating standards are at bighest efficiency.
In travel time, we have shrunk the United States
to the size of Pennsylvania. During the last war
it took five days to cross the continent-now
it is overnight. New York was nearly a full day's
journey from Chicago-now it is less than five
hours.
This saving of time is of incalculable
value to the whole war effort. Thousands of key
men, civilians as well as Army and Navy officers
and Government officials, are saving priceless
hours because they fly.
Not much can be told about it yet, but in addi-
tionto maintaining an extensive domestictransport
system the airlines are flying cargoes and passen-
gers to all parts of the world.
Much of the credit for the airlines' war achieve-
ments must go to their 50,000 men and women:
the mechanics, the pilots, the dispatchers, the
radio operators, the engineers and inspectors,
the meteorologists, the traffic and reservations
personnel, the passenger agents and the steward-
esses, and the many other aircraftsmen who are
serving so vitally in saving time for the nation.
Theirs is a task that requires skill and judgment
and experience. Like the men and women of many
other war industries, they have an important job
to do... and they are doing it well.
